provenance: Original fictional conversations, reviews, and files created for this simulation; not recovered CompuServe archives.

messages.author: Harbor64
messages.subject: DOCK64: can you land with fuel left?
messages.body: I have uploaded DOCK64.BAS, a short numeric docking game for the C64. You begin 30 units above the pad with 30 fuel units. Each turn you choose thrust from zero through five. The display reports altitude, downward speed, and fuel. A landing faster than two units per turn is a crash. There are no machine-code routines or disk writes; the entire game is a BASIC listing.

messages.author: Petunia
messages.subject: RE: DOCK64: can you land with fuel left?
messages.body: First attempt: I spent all my fuel holding position and then fell! The useful clue is that gravity adds two to downward speed each turn. Thrust three reduces that speed by one. I started with thrust two for four turns, then tried three and coasted the final short distance. Keep a paper log of the numbers; it is much easier to understand the second flight.

messages.author: Harbor64
messages.subject: RE: DOCK64: can you land with fuel left?
messages.body: Version 1.1 rejects fractional thrust and values outside zero through five, and limits thrust to the fuel still aboard. The listing is ordinary text, not a tokenized C64 program. Type the numbered lines into BASIC, or use your emulator's text-paste facility, then RUN. C64NOTES.TXT explains that distinction. Post your landing speed and fuel remaining so we can compare flights.

messages.author: WorkbenchWren
messages.subject: A repeatable test beats a drawer full of guesses
messages.body: I keep forgetting which disk I used when a drawing program behaved correctly. My new AMIGALOG.TXT worksheet records the machine, memory, Workbench disk label, application version, extra utilities, and exact steps. I start from the same disk and change one item per run. It is slower than declaring the expansion board guilty, but my notes finally mean something.

messages.author: CopperCat
messages.subject: RE: A repeatable test beats a drawer full of guesses
messages.body: Please include the expected result as well as the observed one. My report said "the picture is wrong," which told the author almost nothing. The useful report was "load the small sample, select the second palette, save under a new name, reopen; the first two colors exchange places." I kept the original drawing untouched and sent the author a copy of the small sample.

messages.author: WorkbenchWren
messages.subject: RE: A repeatable test beats a drawer full of guesses
messages.body: Added fields for expected result, actual result, and whether the problem repeats after a fresh start. There is also space for the name of a backup copy. The worksheet contains no commands and changes no settings. Print it or fill it in with a text editor. Next club night I want us to bring one complete report apiece instead of a bag of unlabeled disks.

messages.author: CopperCat
messages.subject: December postcard exchange: plain characters only
messages.body: PIXELCAT.TXT is my entry for the club postcard exchange: a cat watching a tiny terminal, with a note about keeping each line short. I used ordinary printable characters so the design can travel between our machines. It is deliberately not PETSCII art. Please open it with a fixed-width font and leave the spaces alone.

messages.author: Petunia
messages.subject: RE: December postcard exchange: plain characters only
messages.body: The first copy looked like a collapsed tent because my editor replaced several spaces with a tab. A plain-text copy fixed it. Our exchange rules should be a maximum of 38 columns, no cursor-control sequences, and no dependence on color. That gives the 40-column crowd room to read without horizontal scrolling.

messages.author: Harbor64
messages.subject: RE: December postcard exchange: plain characters only
messages.body: Let us make the next theme "my computer after midnight." Include your handle in the file, but no mailing address. If you adapt the cat, say what you changed. I will collect entries as separate text files so nobody has to extract an unfamiliar archive simply to read a greeting.

messages.author: OrchardAnn
messages.subject: ORCHARD: a basket-counting type-in for club night
messages.body: ORCHARD.BAS gives five rounds of multiplication practice. Each round shows a number of baskets and the apples in each basket. Enter the total; the program keeps your score and shows the right answer after a miss. I used a fixed sequence of problems so a parent can work through the same sheet beside a child. It is an original Applesoft type-in, not a commercial disk.

messages.author: AppleTutor
messages.subject: RE: ORCHARD: a basket-counting type-in for club night
messages.body: This is a good place to demonstrate variables. B holds baskets, A holds apples per basket, and C holds correct answers. Before RUN, use LIST and find the line that compares the answer with A*B. For a younger player, lower the numbers in the two assignment lines. Keep the original listing so the exercise can always be restored.

messages.author: OrchardAnn
messages.subject: RE: ORCHARD: a basket-counting type-in for club night
messages.body: The file includes numbered REM lines identifying the program. Begin with an empty BASIC program and enter the listing exactly; APPLETIP.TXT includes a short checklist. Version 1.1 shows the expected answer after an incorrect response. My club test sheet uses answers 6, 12, 20, 30, and 42. Please mention the version when posting a result.

messages.author: DiskDaisy
messages.subject: What belongs on a disk catalog card?
messages.body: My club disks have labels such as "STUFF" and "MORE STUFF." DISKLOG.TXT is an attempt to retire those names. It has fields for a volume label, date, disk format as reported by the software, program names, and the location of a backup. It also has a separate printer-test log; yesterday's good printout is now clipped to the correct entry.

messages.author: AppleTutor
messages.subject: RE: What belongs on a disk catalog card?
messages.body: Record whether a disk is your master, a working copy, or a disk received from someone else. Do not assume two disks with similar labels contain the same version. I also write down which program created a document, because a filename by itself does not explain how to open it. The catalog should describe what you actually checked.

messages.author: DiskDaisy
messages.subject: RE: What belongs on a disk catalog card?
messages.body: I added a "last checked" line and a place for the application version. Nothing in this form formats or copies a disk. It is a printable worksheet. My next experiment is to catalog ten disks at a time rather than trying to reorganize the entire shelf in one evening.

messages.author: OrchardAnn
messages.subject: A welcome screen for the next user-group meeting
messages.body: APPLEART.TXT is a small welcome card for the December meeting. It fits within 38 columns and uses printable ASCII only. We can show it in a terminal capture or print it at the top of the club handout. The title is fictional, so replace it with your own club's name if you use it.

messages.author: DiskDaisy
messages.subject: RE: A welcome screen for the next user-group meeting
messages.body: I would put the meeting agenda below the picture: introductions, one type-in demonstration, a disk-labeling workshop, and questions. Four short items are easier to read than a screen full of rules. We should also leave a space on the printed copy for the next meeting date.

messages.author: AppleTutor
messages.subject: RE: A welcome screen for the next user-group meeting
messages.body: For the type-in demonstration, use ORCHARD.BAS and invite someone to predict the next pair of numbers before pressing Return. Then show the relevant lines with LIST. The picture makes a friendly opening, but the tiny program gives everyone something they can change and understand.

messages.author: GemGwen
messages.subject: A project folder that the next editor can understand
messages.body: Our club newsletter arrived on three disks with no explanation of which file was final. STDESK.TXT proposes a simple project checklist: original text, working copy, finished copy, a list of assets, and the application version used. The names are suggestions, not a utility that moves files. I want another member to be able to continue the issue without a telephone interrogation.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: RE: A project folder that the next editor can understand
messages.body: Add the page size and font names to the handover note. A file can open successfully and still produce a different page count. Keep an example printout with the project and note which printer produced it. If a font or image is not included, say so explicitly instead of letting the next editor search every disk.

messages.author: GemGwen
messages.subject: RE: A project folder that the next editor can understand
messages.body: The revised checklist has a handover section and a box for missing assets. It also asks for a plain-text copy of the article text. That is useful when two club members have different publishing programs. STCLUB.TXT is our small sample issue, and it can be read without installing any publishing software.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: TEMPO.BAS: quarter-note timing on paper
messages.body: TEMPO.BAS converts beats per minute to the duration of a quarter note in milliseconds and to the length of a four-beat bar in seconds. It is a calculator for ST BASIC, not a MIDI driver or a metronome. At 120 BPM I expect 500 milliseconds per quarter note and two seconds per bar. Enter zero to finish.

messages.author: ClockworkST
messages.subject: RE: TEMPO.BAS: quarter-note timing on paper
messages.body: I tried 60 and 120 first because the answers are easy to check. The display rounds the note duration to one decimal place and the bar duration to two. Remember that the bar calculation assumes four quarter-note beats; it does not infer a time signature from a song name. I would put that assumption directly on the opening screen.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: RE: TEMPO.BAS: quarter-note timing on paper
messages.body: Done in 1.1. The program accepts whole BPM values from 20 through 300 and prints the assumption before asking for input. MIDIPLAN.TXT is a separate rehearsal worksheet for instrument names, channels, patch notes, and cable labels. Neither file sends any MIDI messages or changes an instrument.

messages.author: GemGwen
messages.subject: The ST club newsletter needs small, reproducible projects
messages.body: The sample STCLUB.TXT issue contains a short editor's note, a tempo-calculator exercise, and a project handover checklist. I would rather run one listing that members can understand than promise a large application we never finish. Suggested next issue: bring a one-page account of something you learned while preparing a document or a rehearsal.

messages.author: ClockworkST
messages.subject: RE: The ST club newsletter needs small, reproducible projects
messages.body: A useful submission should include the starting conditions, steps, expected result, and what happened. For a calculator, give two or three inputs with known answers. For a picture or document, include a plain-text explanation of the intended layout. That lets other members distinguish a program error from a missing font or a different setting.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: RE: The ST club newsletter needs small, reproducible projects
messages.body: I volunteer the timing examples: 60 BPM gives 1000 milliseconds and four seconds per four-beat bar; 120 gives 500 and two. The next question is how to explain rounding without making a musician read a mathematics chapter. Keep it short enough to download before the kettle boils.

messages.author: PathPilot
messages.subject: A startup notebook before changing CONFIG.SYS
messages.body: DOSNOTES.TXT is a notebook-style guide to recording a working setup. It explains what PATH and PROMPT do and includes a small example, but it does not install anything. I begin by writing down the DOS version, available memory as reported by my tools, and the programs I need for the task. Then I keep a copy of the original startup files before making one documented change.

messages.author: BatchBeth
messages.subject: RE: A startup notebook before changing CONFIG.SYS
messages.body: Please separate commands typed at the prompt from lines intended for a startup file. That distinction caused most of the confusion at our last club meeting. Your PATH example should also say that its directories must already exist. A path entry does not install the program or create a directory.

messages.author: PathPilot
messages.subject: RE: A startup notebook before changing CONFIG.SYS
messages.body: The guide now labels the examples and explains that PATH replaces the search list when assigned a value. It does not tell members to overwrite their own startup files. My main suggestion is still to record the before-and-after result. A shorter startup file is not an improvement if it omits a driver your application needs.

messages.author: SectorSam
messages.subject: LOSTDISK: a complete tiny adventure in BASIC
messages.body: LOSTDISK.BAS is a small text adventure for GW-BASIC. Search the club room, find a key, open the cabinet, and return the missing demo disk. The commands are numbers so there are no spelling puzzles. It uses no external data files, and it neither reads nor writes your disks. The puzzle state lives in variables until the program ends.

messages.author: BatchBeth
messages.subject: RE: LOSTDISK: a complete tiny adventure in BASIC
messages.body: I tried the cabinet before finding the key and received the locked message, then used the desk and returned to the cabinet. That path works. I also tried returning a disk before collecting it. The program correctly kept me in the room. Five menu options are enough for this exercise; a larger parser would hide the state changes we want beginners to see.

messages.author: SectorSam
messages.subject: RE: LOSTDISK: a complete tiny adventure in BASIC
messages.body: Version 1.1 accepts only whole-number choices from one through five. Please read the REM lines and try adding a second object as a club exercise. The companion CALLCOST.BAS estimates a fictional session cost from minutes and an hourly rate; at 30 minutes and 12 dollars per hour the answer is six dollars. Neither program interacts with the simulator's account balance.

messages.author: BatchBeth
messages.subject: CLUBLIST: a text roster with useful blanks
messages.body: CLUBLIST.TXT contains fictional example entries and a blank record form for a computer club. Each record has a handle, computer, interests, current project, and preferred forum. There are no telephone numbers or home addresses. The file is plain text so it remains readable without a particular database package.

messages.author: PathPilot
messages.subject: RE: CLUBLIST: a text roster with useful blanks
messages.body: I like the project field. "Interested in modems" is vague, while "writing down a repeatable connection test" gives someone a reason to reply. Include a last-updated date so an old request does not look like a current emergency. For a real roster, let members choose what they want included.

messages.author: SectorSam
messages.subject: RE: CLUBLIST: a text roster with useful blanks
messages.body: My example entry points to LOSTDISK.BAS and asks for a different solution path. That connects the roster to something in the library. Next meeting we can pair a first-time programmer with someone who has already typed the listing, and exchange notes through the forum instead of adding everyone to a mailing list.

messages.author: N5SYS
messages.subject: CompuServe Ham Net -- Wednesdays 8 PM Central
messages.body: Welcome to the Amateur Radio Forum! We are starting a weekly CompuServe Ham Net every Wednesday at 8:00 PM Central on the CB simulator, channel 1. Check in with your callsign and location, then join the roundtable -- rigs, packet, antennas, DX, anything ham. All license classes are welcome, from Novice on up. I will serve as net control this week; the job rotates weekly, so volunteers are appreciated. Spread the word on your local repeater! 73, N5SYS.

messages.author: WB5JON
messages.subject: Kantronics KAM impressions after a week
messages.body: My Kantronics KAM arrived last week and I have had it on the air for seven days now. The dual-port design is the real deal: I run VHF packet on 145.01 on one port and HF packet on 14.105 on the other, both at the same time, into my TS-440S. The HF gateway function works nicely, though HF packet is still slow going with the QRM. Mailbox works as advertised. Anyone else running a KAM as a dual-port gateway? I would like to compare notes on HF tuning levels.

messages.author: KA9RTZ
messages.subject: RE: Kantronics KAM impressions after a week
messages.body: I have been running an AEA PK-232 for about six months and it has been rock solid on both VHF and HF packet. The KAM's dual-port trick is tempting, but the PK-232 also does RTTY, AMTOR, CW, and even FAX and SSTV with the right software, which keeps me happy. The new PK-232MBX with the mailbox option looks interesting too. For pure packet work both boxes are fine -- pick the one your local packet crowd can help you configure.

messages.author: N5PKT
messages.subject: Weekly Packet BBS Net -- Saturdays 7 PM Central
messages.body: Announcing a weekly packet net for the forum: every Saturday at 7:00 PM Central on 145.01 MHz through the WB5PKT-7 digipeater here in the Dallas area. Connect your TNC -- Kantronics KAM, AEA PK-232, MFJ-1270, whatever you have -- and join the roundtable. Each week we pick a topic: BBS message forwarding, KA9Q NOS experiments, HF packet techniques, or traffic handling. Out-of-area stations can check in through the HF gateway. Net control this week is N5PKT. 73 and see you on packet!

messages.author: WD5ABC
messages.subject: TS-440S or IC-735? Help me decide
messages.body: I am upgrading from my old TS-520S (tubes still glow, but my back is tired of lifting it) and I have narrowed it down to the Kenwood TS-440S and the Icom IC-735. Both are 100-watt HF all-mode rigs at a similar price. The 440S has the optional internal antenna tuner which appeals to me, and the IC-735 seems to have a slightly better receiver from what I read in the QST reviews. Anyone own one or both? How is the general coverage receive, and which would you buy again? Thanks! -- WD5ABC.

messages.author: K9VHF
messages.subject: RE: TS-440S or IC-735? Help me decide
messages.body: I have owned both, so here is my two cents. The TS-440S with the AT-440 internal tuner is a joy for portable and quick band changes -- push a button and it tunes. The IC-735 has the edge in receiver performance on a crowded 40 meters, and the passband tuning is smoother. If you operate mostly CW and SSB on HF, you cannot go wrong with either. My 440S has been trouble-free for two years. One note: budget for a good power supply and an external speaker for either rig; the internal speakers are small.

messages.author: N5ZZT
messages.subject: FT-757GX mobile installation report
messages.body: Finished installing the Yaesu FT-757GX in my pickup this weekend and I am impressed. The little box does HF plus 6 meters, and the general coverage receiver keeps the XYL happy with broadcast listening on road trips. Running a Hustler resonator set on a ball mount -- 20 and 40 meters so far. Voltage drop was my biggest fight; run heavy cable straight to the battery with fuses at both ends. Worked three states on 40 meter SSB on the drive to work Monday. Mobile HF is a blast.

messages.author: WB5TWR
messages.subject: Rohn 25G vs. free-standing tower?
messages.body: Planning my first real tower this spring: 40 feet with a small tribander and a 2-meter vertical on top. I am torn between Rohn 25G guyed and a free-standing crank-up. The guyed tower is cheaper, but my lot is not huge and guy wires eat yard fast. The crank-up costs more but cranks down for storms and keeps the neighbors calmer. For those who have put up either: what did the concrete base cost you, and would you do it the same way again?

messages.author: KA5ANT
messages.subject: Dipole at 30 feet vs. trap vertical
messages.body: Small lot here and no tower yet, so the choice is a 40-meter dipole at 30 feet between two trees or a trap vertical with a decent radial field. I mostly work 40 and 20 meter SSB and some CW. The dipole is cheap and quiet, but the vertical might hear better on DX. For those who have tried both at modest heights: which got out better for you? I have room for about 30 radials if I go the vertical route.

messages.author: N5DXS
messages.subject: 10 meters is alive -- sunspots doing their thing
messages.body: What a week! With the solar flux climbing as Cycle 22 builds, 10 meters has been open to everywhere during daylight. Worked VK, ZL, and a pile of Europeans on 28.5 MHz SSB with 100 watts to a dipole at 25 feet. If you have not tried 10 lately, spin the dial between 28.4 and 28.6 -- the band sounds like 20 meters did five years ago. This is shaping up to be the best cycle in a decade. Who else is chasing DX on 10?

messages.author: W5CNT
messages.subject: ARRL 10-Meter Contest -- who's on?
messages.body: The ARRL 10-Meter Contest is on right now through Sunday night (0000Z Saturday to 2359Z Sunday). Exchange is signal report and state; DX sends signal report and serial number. With the band in this shape, even a modest station can have a great weekend. I will be on 28.4 to 28.6 SSB and down in the CW portion at 28.05 looking for multipliers. Post your score and best DX here afterward. Good luck and have fun! -- W5CNT.

messages.author: KA9NEW
messages.subject: Studying for General -- 13 wpm code tips?
messages.body: Passed my Technician written last month (the 5 wpm code test was fine) and now I am aiming for General. The 13 wpm code test has me nervous. I copy fine at 10 wpm but fall apart when the speed jumps. What worked for you? I have been copying W1AW code practice in the evenings. Should I just keep at it, or is there a trick to making the jump from 10 to 13? Any study guides worth buying for the General written?

messages.author: N5VE
messages.subject: ARRL/VEC exam session Saturday in Mesquite
messages.body: Reminder: the Dallas Amateur Radio Club is sponsoring an ARRL/VEC exam session this Saturday, December 17, at 9:00 AM at the Red Cross Building, 2300 McKinney Avenue in Dallas. All classes examined -- Novice, Technician, General, Advanced, Extra -- with code tests at 5, 13, and 20 wpm as required. Bring your current license (original and copy), photo ID, and the $4.50 fee. Walk-ins welcome. Talk-in on 146.88. If you have been studying, this is your chance before the holidays!

messages.author: W5ARL
messages.subject: W1AW bulletin and code practice schedule
messages.body: For the newcomers: W1AW, the ARRL headquarters station, sends code practice every weekday evening and bulletins several times a day. Code practice runs at 9 PM Eastern on 3.58, 7.08, 14.07, 21.07, and 28.07 MHz, starting slow and working up to 35 wpm. Bulletins go out on CW, RTTY, and phone. It is the best free code practice there is -- I went from 5 to 13 wpm in four months copying W1AW. Full schedule is in December QST.

messages.author: WB5OLD
messages.subject: FS: Heathkit HW-101, works great
messages.body: For sale: Heathkit HW-101 HF transceiver, built from the kit in the late 70s and still going strong. Full 80-10 meter coverage, SSB and CW, puts out a solid 100 watts. New finals last year, fresh alignment, includes the original manual and a spare set of tubes. Asking $250. Local pickup in the Dallas area preferred -- this thing is heavy. Also have an HM-102 wattmeter for $30. Reply here or catch me on the Wednesday net.

messages.author: K9HT
messages.subject: WTB: 2m handheld -- IC-2AT or FT-209RH
messages.body: Wanted: a 2-meter handheld in good working order. An Icom IC-2AT or Yaesu FT-209RH would be ideal, but I will consider other 2m HTs of similar vintage. Must transmit and receive cleanly; cosmetic wear is fine. I have cash or trade -- I can offer a Kantronics packet TNC (older single-port model) plus cash. Located in Chicago area but I will pay shipping for the right radio. Thanks! -- K9HT.

messages.author: SARGE88
messages.subject: Welcome to the Veterans Forum
messages.body: Welcome, brothers and sisters in arms. This forum is a place for all who served -- Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines, and Coast Guard -- to swap stories, track down old buddies, get straight answers about VA benefits, and remember those who did not come home. Take a look around: Service Stories for your memories, Reunions & Buddy Finder for tracking down your unit, VA Benefits for the latest on the GI Bill and VA programs, and The Wall Remembrance for honoring our fallen. Introduce yourselves and mind your manners -- this is hallowed ground.

messages.author: OMAHA_44
messages.subject: Omaha Beach, June 6, 1944
messages.body: I was nineteen when our Higgins boat dropped its ramp on Omaha Beach. Forty-four years later I can still hear the engines and feel the cold Channel water. Half the boys from my squad never made it past the shingle. I go back every few years to Normandy to stand at the cemetery at Colleville and read the names. To the young folks here: freedom was bought at a price, and I have spent my life trying to be worthy of the men who paid it. God rest them all.

messages.author: CHOSIN50
messages.subject: Chosin Reservoir, winter of 1950
messages.body: Thirty-eight years ago this month we were fighting our way out of the Chosin Reservoir in forty-below cold. Men froze to their sleeping bags. We called ourselves the Chosin Few, and every year there are fewer of us at the reunion. Korea is called the Forgotten War, but nobody who was there has forgotten a thing. If any 1st Marine Division vets from that winter are reading this, I would be proud to hear from you. Semper Fi.

messages.author: HUE_68
messages.subject: Hue City, Tet 1968
messages.body: Twenty years ago this coming February my platoon fought house to house through Hue City. It was the hardest month of my life and the proudest. I lost my best friend on the third day, and I think of him every single day since. Coming home was harder than I expected -- nobody wanted to talk about it then. I am glad there is a place like this now where a man can tell his story among people who understand. Welcome home, brothers. It is never too late to hear it.

messages.author: GRUNT67
messages.subject: Looking for 1/7 Cav buddies, 1967-68
messages.body: Trying to locate anyone who served with B Company, 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry in Vietnam, 1967 to 1968. I was a squad leader, went by the nickname Tex. I have been thinking about Smitty from Ohio and Deacon from Georgia -- we came home on the same freedom bird in March of 68. If you know them or served alongside us, please reply here. Twenty years is too long to lose touch.

messages.author: FLATOP63
messages.subject: USS Enterprise (CVN-65) reunion -- Norfolk, July 1989
messages.body: Mark your calendars: the USS Enterprise Association reunion will be held in Norfolk, Virginia, July 14-16, 1989. All plankowners and crew from every cruise are invited -- bring your families. Events include a memorial service, a tour of the ship if she is in port, and the Saturday night banquet. Dues are $25 per person; contact the association through the address in the latest newsletter. I was aboard for the 1965-66 cruise and would love to see some familiar faces.

messages.author: DOCMEDIC
messages.subject: Searching for 71st Evac Hospital nurses, 1969
messages.body: I was a corpsman with the 71st Evacuation Hospital at Pleiku in 1969, and I have never forgotten the nurses who worked those long nights beside us. I am trying to find Lieutenant Karen M., a surgical nurse from Pennsylvania, and the rest of the night-shift crew. You saved a lot of young lives, and some of us would like to say thank you properly after all these years. Please reply here if you can help.

messages.author: AIRBORNE82
messages.subject: 82nd Airborne Division Assn. reunion, Fayetteville
messages.body: The 82nd Airborne Division Association will hold its annual reunion in Fayetteville, North Carolina, August 10-13, 1989. All paratroopers past and present are welcome, all eras. There will be a memorial ceremony at the division museum, a picnic, and the traditional Saturday dance. Registration is $35 and includes the banquet. I jumped with the 505th in the early 60s and have not missed a reunion in ten years. Airborne, all the way -- hope to see you there.

messages.author: COLLEGEBOUND
messages.subject: Montgomery GI Bill -- how do I apply?
messages.body: I got out of the Army in June and want to start college in January using the Montgomery GI Bill. I had the $100 a month taken out of my pay for my first twelve months in, so I should be eligible under the 1984 law. What is the actual process? Do I apply through the VA regional office first, or enroll in school and let the school certify me? Any advice from someone who has already navigated the paperwork would be appreciated. I want to get this right the first time.

messages.author: HOMESTEAD
messages.subject: VA home loan questions
messages.body: My wife and I are looking at our first house and I want to use my VA home loan benefit. I served four years in the Navy, honorable discharge in 1984. Am I correct that there is no down payment required and no private mortgage insurance? Also, can the entitlement be reused if I sell the house later? The lender I talked to did not seem to know much about VA loans, so I would rather hear from veterans who have actually used one. Thanks in advance.

messages.author: JUNGLE69
messages.subject: Agent Orange Registry exam -- my experience
messages.body: For anyone who served in Vietnam and has been putting it off: I finally went in for my Agent Orange Registry exam at the VA medical center last month. It is free, it took about half a day, and the doctor went through a full history and physical. The registry was set up so the VA can track health effects, and getting the exam on record is the smart move whether you feel fine or not. Call your local VA and ask for the Agent Orange coordinator -- they will schedule you. Take care of yourselves, brothers.

messages.author: DAKTO67
messages.subject: VA medical care eligibility?
messages.body: Question for the group: I have a service-connected knee injury rated at 30 percent from Vietnam, 1967. Am I eligible for VA medical care for the knee only, or for general care too? I have been paying out of pocket for everything and only just learned I might qualify for treatment at the VA hospital. Also, is there a means test involved these days? I do not want to take a slot from someone who needs it more, but my knee is getting worse. Straight answers appreciated.

messages.author: BROTHERINK
messages.subject: Found my buddy's name on the Wall
messages.body: I finally made the trip to Washington last month and stood before the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. I found my buddy Danny on Panel 23E, and I made a rubbing of his name to bring home to his mother. The Wall is exactly as powerful as everyone says -- 58,000 names, and every one of them somebody's son or daughter. I left my unit patch at the base of his panel. If you have never been, go. It heals something in you.

messages.author: PANEL23E
messages.subject: Rubbing request -- Panel 12W, Line 114
messages.body: Is anyone planning a trip to Washington, D.C., soon? I am hoping someone can make a pencil rubbing of a name on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial for me: Panel 12W, Line 114. He was my platoon sergeant in 1968, and I cannot make the trip myself this year. I will gladly cover postage and supplies. Please reply here if you can help -- it would mean the world to his family and to me.

messages.author: VIGILANT
messages.subject: Veterans Day at the Wall
messages.body: I spent Veterans Day, November 11th, at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial this year, and I wanted to share it with those who could not be there. Hundreds of us stood in the cold as the wreaths were laid and the names of the fallen were read. Strangers helped each other find panels. A Gold Star mother next to me was tracing her son's name with her fingertip, and not a dry eye in sight. We remember them. We will always remember them.

messages.author: CANDLELIGHT
messages.subject: A candle for the MIAs
messages.body: This Christmas season, I am lighting a candle for the men still listed as missing in action -- ours and every family's who never got an answer. The Wall carries their names too, marked with the cross that means missing, and their families visit those panels with the same grief and the same pride. Until every one of them is accounted for, we keep the faith and we keep their memory alive. You are not forgotten.

messages.author: RootsSysop
messages.subject: Welcome to Roots & Branches -- read this first
messages.body:
Welcome to the Roots & Branches Genealogy Forum! Whether you are chasing your first family line or you have been at this for twenty years, you will find help here. A few ground rules and suggestions:

1. Start with yourself and work backward, one generation at a time. Record full names, dates, and places on pedigree charts and family group sheets.
2. Talk to your oldest relatives NOW, while you can. A tape-recorded interview beats a courthouse record every time.
3. Cite your sources. 'Grandma said so' is a clue, not proof.
4. Use the Surname Registry section to post the names you are researching -- surname, dates, and place.

Browse the section list, introduce yourself, and happy hunting!

messages.author: FamilySleuth
messages.subject: New to genealogy -- where do I actually begin?
messages.body: I want to trace my family but I am overwhelmed. I have my grandparents' names and not much else. Where do I start without spending a fortune? Is there a book or magazine that explains the basics? I live near Dallas if that matters for libraries or archives. Any advice for a total beginner would be appreciated.

messages.author: RootsSysop
messages.subject: RE: New to genealogy -- where do I actually begin?
messages.body:
FamilySleuth, here is the standard beginner drill:

1. Fill out a pedigree chart starting with yourself. Interview parents, aunts, uncles -- ask about full names (including maiden names), birth/marriage/death dates and places.
2. Gather home sources: family Bibles, old letters, photo albums, funeral cards, military discharge papers.
3. Get a beginner book. The public library will have several; ask the reference desk for the genealogy shelf. Everton's Genealogical Helper magazine is a good monthly to browse.
4. Write to county courthouses for birth, marriage, and death certificates -- always enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope (SASE) and the fee.
5. Visit your nearest LDS Family History Center (see the Family History Centers section) -- the volunteers will get you onto microfilm fast.

Work backward one generation at a time and document everything.

messages.author: PaperTrail
messages.subject: Organizing paper files -- binders vs. file folders?
messages.body: After a year of collecting, I am drowning in paper: census printouts from the microfilm reader, courthouse letters, photocopies of pension files. How do you all organize? I am torn between a binder per surname and plain manila folders in a file cabinet. Also, do you keep a research log? I keep re-searching the same microfilm rolls because I forgot I already looked. There has to be a better system.

messages.author: LoneStarRoots
messages.subject: Which NARA regional archive holds my records?
messages.body: I need naturalization and federal court records for ancestors in Texas and Oklahoma. I know the National Archives has regional branches -- is there one near Dallas? More generally, how do I find out which regional archive covers which states before I write or drive over? I would rather not guess wrong and waste a trip.

messages.author: ArchivalDan
messages.subject: RE: Which NARA regional archive holds my records?
messages.body: LoneStarRoots, you are in luck: the National Archives regional branch in Fort Worth serves Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Louisiana, so your people are covered right there. Each regional archive publishes a guide to its holdings -- write ahead and ask for it, and describe the records you want so the staff can confirm they hold them. For military and pension files, though, those stay in Washington -- you order copies by mail on the NATF forms (see the Military Records section). Always write first; the archivists will tell you exactly what to bring.

messages.author: CensusTaker
messages.subject: Soundex microfilm -- how do I actually use it?
messages.body: I finally sat down at a microfilm reader with the Soundex index and felt lost. I am looking for my great-grandfather in the 1900 census, surname KOWALSKI in Illinois. Can someone walk me through the Soundex coding? I know it groups similar-sounding names, but how do I turn KOWALSKI into a code, and what do I do with the code once I have it? The 1900 and 1910 censuses are Soundexed (and 1880 partially), right?

messages.author: BrickWallBetty
messages.subject: RE: Soundex microfilm -- how do I actually use it?
messages.body: CensusTaker, the Soundex is your best friend once it clicks. Take the first letter of the surname (K), then code the consonants: KOWALSKI becomes K-420. Find the microfilm roll for the state and code range, then scan the cards alphabetically by given name within the code. Each card gives the enumeration district, sheet, and line -- then you pull the actual census roll. Yes: Soundex microfilm exists for the 1880 (partial), 1900, and 1910 censuses at NARA and most large libraries. Bring dimes for the reader-printer -- you will want copies.

messages.author: OhioBound
messages.subject: 1890 census destroyed -- what are the workarounds?
messages.body: Just learned the hard way that the 1890 federal census was destroyed in a 1921 fire -- the one census I needed most, of course. My Ohio family vanishes between 1880 and 1900. What do experienced researchers use as a substitute for 1890? I have heard mention of a special veterans schedule and city directories. What actually works?

messages.author: BuckeyeGene
messages.subject: RE: 1890 census destroyed -- what are the workarounds?
messages.body:
OhioBound, the 1890 gap is every genealogist's rite of passage. Substitutes that actually work:

- The special 1890 schedule of Union veterans and widows survives for about half the states -- check if Ohio's is on microfilm at your library.
- City directories for 1890-1891 list addresses and occupations year by year.
- Tax lists, voter registrations, and church records.
- State censuses: some states took their own (Ohio did not in 1890, unfortunately).
- County histories with biographical sketches.

Layer two or three of these and you can usually bridge the 1880-1900 gap.

messages.author: UtahBound
messages.subject: First visit to a Family History Center -- what to expect?
messages.body: There is an LDS Family History Center twenty minutes from me and I finally want to go. What should I expect? Do I need to be a church member? Can I just walk in and use the microfilm readers? I have a list of rolls I want from the Family History Library Catalog -- can they get them, and what does it cost? Any etiquette tips so I do not embarrass myself on day one?

messages.author: MicrofilmMabel
messages.subject: RE: First visit to a Family History Center -- what to expect?
messages.body: UtahBound, welcome aboard! The centers are open to everyone, no membership needed, and the volunteers are wonderful. You can order any microfilm listed in the Family History Library Catalog on microfiche -- rental is a few dollars per roll and the film stays at the center for several weeks. Call ahead for hours, since most are staffed by volunteers. Bring a notebook, pencils (no pens near the readers, please), and coins for the copy machine. Start with the IGI on microfiche -- the International Genealogical Index -- to see if your surnames are already extracted.

messages.author: ChicagoRoots
messages.subject: Surname registry: KOWALSKI, Chicago 1880-1920
messages.body:
Posting to the registry per the sysop's instructions:

Surname: KOWALSKI (also spelled KOWALSKY, KOVALSKI)
Place: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois
Dates: arrived about 1882, in Chicago by the 1900 census
Seeking: parents of STANLEY KOWALSKI (b. ~1860 Poland), marriage record to MARY NOWAK (~1885, St. Stanislaus parish?), and the passenger list for the 1882 arrival.

Willing to trade lookups in Chicago-area microfilm. Contact me here in the forum.

messages.author: CorkToBoston
messages.subject: Surname registry: SULLIVAN, County Cork to Boston
messages.body:
Surname: SULLIVAN (O'SULLIVAN in some records)
Place: Skibbereen parish, County Cork, Ireland -> Boston, Massachusetts
Dates: emigrated about 1849-1851, in Boston by 1860 census
Seeking: baptismal records for DANIEL SULLIVAN (b. ~1825) and wife HONORA, passenger arrival record (Boston, ~1850), and any connection to Sullivans remaining in Skibbereen.

I have Boston city directories 1860-1880 on microfilm notes and will gladly share lookups.

messages.author: RevWarRick
messages.subject: Revolutionary War pension files -- what is actually in them?
messages.body: I am thinking of ordering my 4th-great-grandfather's Revolutionary War pension file from the National Archives. Before I send the NATF Form 80 and the fee, what can I expect to get? Are these just a few pages, or can they really run to dozens of pages? I have heard they sometimes include family details you cannot find anywhere else.

messages.author: PensionFileFan
messages.subject: RE: Revolutionary War pension files -- what is actually in them?
messages.body: RevWarRick, order it -- pension files are genealogy gold. A Revolutionary War pension file (the M804 microfilm series) can run 20 to 60 pages: the veteran's own narrative of his service, affidavits from comrades, marriage records, children's birth dates, and sometimes letters in the widow's hand. The NATF Form 80 costs $10 and you mail it to Washington. Be patient -- turnaround is several weeks. One file broke a ten-year brick wall for me with a single deposition naming four siblings.

messages.author: DraftDigger
messages.subject: WWI draft cards on microfilm -- anyone used them?
messages.body: I found out my great-grandfather's WWI draft registration card is on microfilm (the M1509 series, I think). For those who have used them: what information is actually on the card? I am hoping for a birth date and physical description. Are these at NARA regional branches, or do I need to go through the Family History Center? Any tips for finding the right roll?

messages.author: ServiceRecordSam
messages.subject: RE: WWI draft cards on microfilm -- anyone used them?
messages.body: DraftDigger, the WWI draft cards are fantastic -- nearly every man born roughly 1872-1900 registered, so coverage is excellent. Each card gives full name, home address, birth date and place, occupation and employer, nearest relative, and a physical description including height, build, and eye and hair color. The M1509 microfilm is at NARA and many large libraries and Family History Centers -- the rolls are arranged by state, then county and draft board. Bring the 1910 or 1900 census entry so you know which board's roll to pull.

messages.author: SixStringSysop
messages.subject: Welcome to the Guitar & Music Forum
messages.body: Welcome, pickers and grinners. This is the place to talk guitars: electrics, acoustics, amps, pedals, and everything with strings. We have sections for gear talk, a tablature exchange (post your own transcriptions, note the tuning), a MIDI and home-recording corner for the Portastudio crowd, and a What's Spinning section for whatever is on your turntable this month. Introduce yourself, list your rig, and mind the house rule: no flame wars about tonewood. Play nice.

messages.author: STRATCAT
messages.subject: American Standard Strat vs. '62 reissue?
messages.body: I am finally buying a real Strat and I am torn between the new American Standard and a '62 vintage reissue. The American Standard has the 2-point trem and the hotter bridge pickup, and the necks feel great, but there is something about the reissue's 7.25-inch radius and vintage frets. I play mostly blues-rock and some clean funk. Anyone A/B'd them? Is the reissue worth the extra money, or is that paying for the headstock decal?

messages.author: BURSTBELIEVER
messages.subject: Les Paul Standard -- how heavy is too heavy?
messages.body: Tried three Les Paul Standards at the shop yesterday. The honeyburst weighed a ton but sustained for days; the lighter one felt better on the shoulder but sounded thinner. All had the Tim Shaw-era pickups. For those gigging a Paul: what is your weight limit, and does a wide strap really save your back on a four-set night? Also, anyone compared the '57 Goldtop reissue to the Standard? That P-90 growl is calling my name.

messages.author: FLATPICKER
messages.subject: D-28 vs. J-45 for bluegrass flatpicking
messages.body: Saving up for a lifetime dreadnought and I have it narrowed to a Martin D-28 and a Gibson J-45. I play mostly bluegrass rhythm and some flatpicked leads. The D-28 has that piano-like bass and cuts through a jam; the J-45 is warmer and records beautifully but can get lost next to a banjo. For those who own one or the other: which did you choose and why? And what strings are you running -- phosphor bronze lights, or do you go medium for the volume?

messages.author: CHURCHGIG
messages.subject: Takamine with the built-in pickup -- gig-worthy?
messages.body: I play acoustic at church and small coffeehouses and I am tired of fighting feedback with a soundhole pickup. The Takamine EF series with the built-in palathetic pickup keeps coming up -- under-saddle, preamp in the side, feedback-resistant. Anyone gigging one? How does it sound through a PA versus miked with an SM57? I do not want that quacky piezo tone if I can avoid it.

messages.author: STACKATTACK
messages.subject: JCM800 2204 vs. 2203 -- 50W or 100W?
messages.body: Looking at a used Marshall JCM800 and I cannot decide between the 50-watt 2204 and the 100-watt 2203. I play clubs, not arenas, and I want power-tube grind without killing the front row. The 50-watter breaks up earlier and weighs less, but everybody says the 100-watt has bigger iron and tighter bass. For those running a 2204: do you miss the headroom? And where do you set the preamp vs. master for classic rock crunch?

messages.author: CLEANMACHINE
messages.subject: JC-120 as a pedal platform
messages.body: Considering a Roland JC-120 Jazz Chorus as the foundation for a pedalboard rig. The clean headroom is legendary and the stereo chorus is gorgeous, but it is solid-state -- will my Tube Screamer and RAT still feel right through it? I play in a Top 40 band and need pristine cleans plus convincing dirt at moderate volume. Anyone running dirt pedals into a JC-120 nightly? How does it take a DS-1?

messages.author: TEXASBLUES
messages.subject: Tube Screamer into a Twin Reverb -- settings?
messages.body: Got an Ibanez TS-9 Tube Screamer to push my Twin Reverb into blues territory. The Twin stays clean forever, which is the point, but I am still dialing in the Screamer: drive at 9 o'clock, tone at noon, level maxed seems to be the classic recipe. What are your TS-9 settings? And for SRV-style bite, do you stack a second boost or just dig in harder? Using a Strat with stock single coils, by the way.

messages.author: TABTRADER
messages.subject: TAB: Sultans of Swing -- intro (standard tuning)
messages.body:
By request, here is my transcription of the Sultans of Swing intro. Standard tuning, clean Strat on the neck+middle pickup, fingerpicked.

E||-------------------------|---------------------------|
B||-------------------------|---------------------------|
G||--------7-----7-----7----|--------7-----7-----7--------|
D||-----7-----7-----7-----7-|-----7-----7-----7-----7-----|
A||--5---------------------|--5--------------------------|
E||-------------------------|---------------------------|

That is the skeleton -- Knopfler's fills dance around the D major shape. Corrections welcome; I worked this out by ear off the vinyl. Next up if there is interest: the Money for Nothing riff.

messages.author: JUNGLEJIM
messages.subject: Request: Sweet Child O' Mine intro tab
messages.body: Can anyone post a tab for the Sweet Child O' Mine intro? I have the D-C-G-D shape down but Slash's embellishments are faster than my ear. Standard tuning, and I know he plays it on the neck pickup of a Les Paul. Even a rough sketch of the first four bars would help. Happy to trade -- I have clean tabs for the Hotel California solo and the Stairway intro if anyone needs them.

messages.author: MIDIMAN
messages.subject: Layering DX7 and D-50 -- MIDI channel setup
messages.body: Finally have both a Yamaha DX7 and a Roland D-50 in the home studio and I want to layer them from one keyboard. The plan: DX7 as master on channel 1, D-50 receiving on channel 1 with local off, then split the D-50's upper/lower across two channels for sequencer overdubs. For those running a two-keyboard MIDI rig: any gotchas with the D-50's patch changes eating the DX7's program changes? And is anyone using a dedicated MIDI patchbay, or just daisy-chaining thru ports?

messages.author: FOURTRACK
messages.subject: Syncing HR-16 drum machine to Portastudio 244
messages.body: Home recording question: I am tracking on a TASCAM Portastudio 244 (4-track cassette) and I want my Alesis HR-16 drum machine to stay in sync across takes. I know the 244 has no MIDI sync, so I am striping SMPTE-ish sync tone from a JL Cooper box to track 4 and slaving the HR-16 to it. It works, but I lose a track. Is there a better way short of buying a bigger machine? How are the rest of you syncing drums to cassette 4-tracks?

messages.author: SYNTHAXE
messages.subject: Guitar synth live -- Casio PG-380 impressions?
messages.body: Anyone gigging a guitar synth? I tried the Casio PG-380 (Strat-style with the built-in synth module) at the shop and the tracking was better than I expected -- the brass and string patches actually followed my playing. My worry is live reliability and whether the synth sounds sit in a band mix or just sound like a novelty. For studio layering it seems like a no-brainer at the price. Talk me into it or out of it.

messages.author: THRASHFAN
messages.subject: ...And Justice for All -- where is the bass?
messages.body: Been living with the new Metallica record for three months now and I have to ask: where is the bass guitar? You can hear Newsted on exactly none of it -- the whole album is guitars, drums, and Hetfield's voice fighting for the same midrange. One is a masterpiece of arrangement, but the mix is so dry it hurts. Am I crazy, or did they bury the new guy on purpose? Still, that title track's middle section is the heaviest thing I have heard all year.

messages.author: DESERTROCK
messages.subject: Rattle and Hum -- film and album
messages.body: Caught Rattle and Hum last weekend and picked up the double album after. The Sun Studios sessions are the highlight for me -- the band sounds loose and alive in a way the Joshua Tree tour sometimes was not. The BB King collaboration on When Love Comes to Town gave me chills. Is it self-indulgent? Sure, a little. But as a document of a band at the absolute peak of its powers, I am glad it exists. What is everyone else spinning this month?

messages.author: FINGERSTYLE
messages.subject: Tracy Chapman -- Fast Car fingerpicking
messages.body: The Tracy Chapman debut has been on my turntable all month, and Fast Car is a masterclass in less-is-more guitar: that rolling Travis-picked pattern under the whole song, capo up, never a wasted note. For the fingerstyle players here: are you playing it with thumbpick and fingers, or bare thumb? I am getting the pattern clean at tempo but the bass notes keep overpowering the melody. Also, Talkin' 'bout a Revolution uses the same vocabulary -- great study piece for beginners.

files.content:
10 REM DOCK64 1.1 - ORIGINAL CLUB TYPE-IN
20 H=30:V=3:F=30
30 PRINT "DOCK64 - LAND AT SPEED 2 OR LESS"
40 PRINT "DOWNWARD SPEED IS POSITIVE"
50 PRINT "HEIGHT";H;" SPEED";V

reviews.author: Harbor64
reviews.text: The distinction between ASCII listings and PRG files saves beginners a confusing LOAD attempt.

files.content:
C64 TYPE-IN DESK - ORIGINAL CLUB NOTES

A text listing and a saved BASIC program are different things. The .BAS
files in this collection contain printable numbered lines. They are not
tokenized PRG files and are not disk images. Start with an empty BASIC
program, enter the lines, and use LIST to inspect the result before RUN.
An emulator may offer a text-paste facility; consult its instructions.

Each line number identifies a line. Entering a replacement with the same
number replaces that line. Keep a copy of the original listing before
experimenting. DOCK64 uses PRINT for display, INPUT for a number, and
IF ... THEN to select a branch. A colon separates statements on one line.

DOCK64 CHECK FLIGHT
Enter thrust 2 four times: heights 27, 24, 21, 18; speed stays 3.
Then enter 3: height 16, speed 2. Enter 2 eight times to land gently.
The ending should report 3 fuel and a safe landing at speed 2.
Try a different sequence and record height, speed, and fuel each turn.

The listing uses no graphics, sound, device access, POKE, or machine code.
Reference: Commodore 64 Programmer's Reference Guide, BASIC chapters.
https://www.commodore.ca/manuals/c64_programmers_reference/c64-programmers_reference.htm
These are newly written notes, not a transcription of the manual.

files.description: Five rounds of basket-and-apple arithmetic practice.
files.instructions: ASCII source listing, not a tokenized disk image. Enter numbered lines in the named BASIC interpreter, then RUN. Programs are original simulation content.
history: 1.1: Show the correct total after a miss.

reviews.author: AppleTutor
reviews.text: Known answers make this a useful first type-in and a simple variables lesson.

files.content:
10 REM ORCHARD 1.1 - ORIGINAL TYPE-IN
20 C=0
30 PRINT "ORCHARD - FIVE COUNTING ROUNDS"
40 FOR R=1 TO 5
50 B=R+1:A=R+2
60 PRINT "BASKETS: ";B
70 PRINT "APPLES IN EACH: ";A
80 INPUT "TOTAL APPLES";N
90 IF N=A*B THEN 120
100 PRINT "THE TOTAL IS ";A*B
110 GOTO 140
120 PRINT "CORRECT!"
130 C=C+1
140 NEXT R
150 PRINT "CORRECT ANSWERS: ";C;" OF 5"
160 END

files.name: APPLETIP.TXT
files.description: Applesoft type-in checklist and ORCHARD exercises.
files.instructions: Open in a plain-text editor or print with a fixed-width font. Original simulation content; no installation needed.

reviews.author: OrchardAnn
reviews.text: A short lesson that can be printed beside the computer.

files.content:
APPLESOFT TYPE-IN CHECKLIST
Original Apple II Forum workshop sheet.

1. Keep your existing work before starting an empty BASIC program.
2. Enter each numbered line of ORCHARD.BAS exactly as shown.
3. LIST the program. Check line numbers, quotation marks, and punctuation.
4. RUN. The five expected totals are 6, 12, 20, 30, and 42.
5. An all-correct run reports 5 OF 5. Five zero answers report 0 OF 5.

The downloadable .BAS file is an ASCII listing. It is not a tokenized
Applesoft program or a bootable Apple disk. Use a text-paste feature only
if your emulator supports it; otherwise type the numbered lines.

READING THE PROGRAM
R is the round. B is baskets. A is apples per basket. N is the answer.
C counts correct answers. FOR and NEXT repeat the rounds. IF tests the
answer, and GOTO skips the success message after a wrong answer.

EXERCISES
Change line 50 so every basket contains two apples.
Write down all five expected answers before running the changed version.
Change the opening message. Keep the double quotes around the text.
Restore the original listing and verify the original five answers again.

The program performs no disk operations and uses no graphics commands.
Reference: Apple's Applesoft BASIC programming manuals; these notes and
the exercise are original simulation material, not archived forum posts.

files.content:
ST DESKTOP PROJECT HANDOVER
Original checklist for a club newsletter or short document.

PROJECT TITLE:
EDITOR / HANDLE:
APPLICATION / VERSION:
ORIGINAL TEXT FILE:
WORKING DOCUMENT:
FINISHED DOCUMENT:
PAGE SIZE / MARGINS:
FONT NAMES:
PICTURE FILES:
PRINTER / EXAMPLE PRINTOUT:

Include a plain-text copy of the article text when practical. Record any
fonts or pictures that are not supplied with the project. Keep the working
copy separate from the finished copy and explain which is which.

BEFORE HANDOVER
[ ] Open the finished document and inspect each page.
[ ] Compare the page count with the example printout.
[ ] Check that filenames in the handover note match the actual files.
[ ] Describe any missing assets or unresolved layout problems.
[ ] Ask another member to read the note without verbal explanations.

This checklist does not move files, install fonts, or change the desktop.

MUSIC WORKSHOP - REHEARSAL PLAN
Original blank worksheet. This file sends no MIDI commands.

Piece:                           Date:
Tempo (BPM):                     Time signature:
Instrument name:
Receive channel (check instrument manual):
Patch / sound name:
Patch numbering convention used by this instrument:
Cable label and destination:
Who controls starting and stopping:

BEFORE REHEARSAL
Record the starting settings. Check one instrument at a time. Write down
the sound name as well as a patch number; two instruments may label their
sounds differently. Keep notes for the next session.

TEMPO.BAS CHECKS
60 BPM -> 1000 milliseconds per quarter note.
120 BPM -> 500 milliseconds per quarter note.
The program's bar duration assumes four quarter-note beats.
It is a duration calculator, not a timing source or metronome.

AFTER REHEARSAL
What worked:
What changed:
Settings to restore next time:

reviews.author: ClockworkST
reviews.text: Short enough to read in one sitting and tied to files actually in this library.

files.content:
THE SMALL SCREEN - DECEMBER 1988
An original fictional Atari ST club newsletter.

FROM THE EDITOR
This month's rule is simple: bring a project another member can finish.
A folder full of unexplained files is a puzzle, not a handover. Include a
short note, the application version, and an example of the intended result.

WORKSHOP: TIME ON PAPER
Our TEMPO.BAS type-in answers two questions: how long is one quarter note,
and how long is a bar containing four of them? At 120 BPM the answers are
500 milliseconds and two seconds. Try 60 BPM, then explain why both
durations doubled. The program does not operate your instruments.

DESKTOP DESK
The next editor may not own your fonts. STDESK.TXT asks you to identify
missing assets and include plain article text. A printout can explain a
layout more quickly than three telephone calls about the second column.

NEXT MEETING
Bring one short project, a known result, and a question. We will pair
members and see whether each can reproduce the other's result from notes.
No prize for the largest pile of disks; applause for the clearest notes.

files.name: CALLCOST.BAS
files.description: Estimate fictional connect charges from minutes and rate.
files.instructions: ASCII source listing, not a tokenized disk image. Enter numbered lines in the named BASIC interpreter, then RUN. Programs are original simulation content.

reviews.author: PathPilot
reviews.text: 30 minutes at 12 per hour reports 6. The estimate never changes account billing.

files.content:
10 REM CALLCOST 1.1 - FICTIONAL ESTIMATE
20 PRINT "SESSION COST - NO ACCOUNT CHANGES"
30 INPUT "MINUTES, 0 TO END";M
40 IF M=0 THEN 130
50 IF M<0 OR M>1440 THEN 30
60 INPUT "HOURLY RATE 0 TO 100";R
70 IF R<0 OR R>100 THEN 60
80 C=M*R/60
90 C=INT(C*100+.5)/100
100 PRINT "ESTIMATED DOLLARS: ";C
110 PRINT "NO SURCHARGES OR TAX INCLUDED"
120 GOTO 30
130 END

history: 1.1: Reject invalid and fractional menu choices.

reviews.author: BatchBeth
reviews.text: Try the locked cabinet first. Then inspect the desk, revisit the cabinet, and return the disk.

files.content:
10 REM LOSTDISK 1.1 - ORIGINAL ADVENTURE
20 K=0:D=0
30 PRINT "THE CLUB DEMO DISK IS MISSING."
40 PRINT "1 DESK  2 CABINET  3 NOTICE"
50 PRINT "4 RETURN DISK  5 QUIT"
60 INPUT "CHOICE";C
70 IF C<1 OR C>5 OR C<>INT(C) THEN 60
80 ON C GOTO 100,140,200,230,290
100 PRINT "A BRASS KEY IS UNDER THE NOTES."
110 K=1
120 GOTO 40
140 IF K=0 THEN 180
150 PRINT "THE KEY FITS. YOU TAKE THE DISK."
160 D=1
170 GOTO 40
180 PRINT "THE CABINET IS LOCKED."
190 GOTO 40
200 PRINT "NOTICE: THE DEMO STARTS AT EIGHT."
210 PRINT "PLEASE RETURN THE CLUB DISK."
220 GOTO 40
230 IF D=0 THEN 270
240 PRINT "YOU RETURN THE DISK. SHOW SAVED!"
250 END
270 PRINT "YOU DO NOT HAVE THE DISK YET."
280 GOTO 40
290 PRINT "YOU LEAVE THE CLUB ROOM."
300 END

files.content:
DOS WORKSHOP NOTEBOOK
Original notes, not an automatic setup script.

RECORD FIRST
DOS version:
Application and version:
Current startup-file backup location:
Available memory as reported by your tools:
Driver or resident programs required for this task:
One proposed change and expected result:

EXAMPLES TYPED AT A DOS PROMPT
PROMPT $P$G
  Displays the current drive and directory followed by >.
PATH C:\DOS;C:\UTIL
  Example search list only. These directories must already exist and
  contain your programs. Assigning PATH replaces its existing search
  list; it does not create directories or install software.

Keep a working copy of your own startup files before editing them. Make
one change, record the result, and retain the configuration your required
applications need. These notes do not supply a replacement CONFIG.SYS.

GW-BASIC FILES
CALLCOST.BAS and LOSTDISK.BAS are ASCII source. From GW-BASIC in the
directory containing a listing, use LOAD "LOSTDISK.BAS" and then RUN.
LOAD replaces the program currently in memory, so save your work first.
The examples do not access files or change the simulator account.

CALLCOST CHECK: 30 minutes at 12 per hour is 6 dollars. Zero minutes ends.
LOSTDISK CHECK: choices 1, 2, 4 solve the puzzle; choice 5 quits.
